chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi and Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who is muqatib (a slave contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) who dies and has paid some of his contract amount, and he has a son from his slave girl: He (peace be upon him) said: 'If it was stipulated upon him that if he was unable (to pay), he would remain a slave, then his son returns as a slave along with the slave girl; and if it was not stipulated upon him, his son pays what remains of the contract amount and inherits what remains.'

key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has contracted with his master to pay a specific sum for his freedom
key_terms.مُكَاتَبَتِهِ: The contract of manumission or the amount agreed upon for freedom

ai.seo_question: What happens to the son of a deceased contracted slave if the master stipulated reversion to slavery upon inability to pay?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the legal status of the son of a muqatib's concubine, distinguishing between conditional reversion to slavery and unconditional inheritance based on the master's stipulation. It highlights the Shia juristic principle that contractual conditions dictate the transmission of both debt and status, ensuring the master's rights are preserved while allowing the son to secure freedom through payment. This case study is foundational in understanding the interplay between manumission contracts (kitabah) and inheritance laws in classical fiqh.
